label: Roman Republic & Empire
summary: Rome developed from a republic into an empire in 27 BCE. Roads, aqueducts, baths and amphitheatres connected its provinces. The 476 endpoint refers to western imperial rule; the eastern empire continued.
sourceName: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Roman Art: A Resource for Educators
geographyNote: Representative present-day locations of Roman remains, not fixed imperial borders.

label: Classical Greek city-states
summary: Independent and competing city-states shared Greek language and religious traditions. Temples, theatres and civic spaces expressed communal identity. This cultural period ends conventionally with Alexander the Great's death, not the disappearance of Greek culture.
sourceName: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · The Art of Classical Greece
geographyNote: Greek mainland and islands, with Greek communities in southern Italy and western Anatolia.

label: Hellenistic kingdoms & cities
summary: After Alexander's death, successor kingdoms supported monumental architecture and expanded Greek cultural networks. The conventional endpoint is the Battle of Actium; Greek artistic traditions continued under Rome.
sourceName: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Art of the Hellenistic Age
geographyNote: European and Mediterranean places in a cultural network extending far beyond Europe.

label: Eastern Roman / Byzantine Empire
summary: The Roman state centred on Constantinople developed a distinctive Christian court and architectural tradition. Domed churches and mosaics are key clues. Its territory changed greatly, and Byzantine rule in Constantinople was interrupted from 1204 to 1261.
sourceName: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Byzantium (ca. 330–1453)
geographyNote: Representative locations of Byzantine rule or major Byzantine heritage; not continuous occupation.

label: Medieval Latin Christian Europe
summary: A broad context for many distinct kingdoms, towns and religious communities. Monasteries, castles and cathedrals reveal overlapping political and spiritual authority. Romanesque and Gothic buildings belong to different phases within this long period.
sourceName: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Medieval Art: A Resource for Educators
geographyNote: A cultural overview of western and central Europe, not a single state or a claim of religious uniformity.
dateNote: Rounded overview dates; regional transitions into and out of the Middle Ages differ.

label: Al-Andalus
summary: Changing Muslim-ruled territories in Iberia included successive emirates, caliphates and kingdoms. Córdoba's mosque and Granada's palaces help connect court patronage, water and ornament. Al-Andalus was never one unchanged state.
sourceName: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Art of Islamic Spain
geographyNote: Iberian territories changed over time; the final Nasrid kingdom centred on Granada.

label: Carolingian courts & revival
summary: Charlemagne's reign and later Carolingian patronage revived Roman and early Christian models. Aachen's chapel expresses imperial ambition. The cultural range shown here extends beyond the empire's political fragmentation.
sourceName: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Carolingian Art
geographyNote: Frankish western and central Europe; Aachen is a principal architectural anchor.
dateNote: Begins with Charlemagne's accession in 768; 900 is a rounded cultural endpoint. Imperial coronation occurred in 800.

label: Holy Roman Empire
summary: A changing imperial framework linked many principalities, bishoprics and free cities. Its buildings span medieval churches, civic halls and Baroque courts. It was a different institution from ancient Rome and had no single fixed territorial outline.
sourceName: Deutsches Historisches Museum · Holy Roman Empire, 962–1806
geographyNote: Representative modern locations within the empire at different times, not its borders in every year.

label: Ottoman Empire
summary: An empire founded in Anatolia expanded into southeastern Europe in the fourteenth century. Mosques, bridges, baths and markets record its urban legacy. The dates describe the empire as a whole; European regions entered and left Ottoman rule at different times.
sourceName: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · The Greater Ottoman Empire
geographyNote: Present-day locations of Ottoman rule and heritage; Romania includes vassal principalities rather than uniform direct rule.

label: Italian Renaissance cities & courts
summary: Competing Italian republics, courts and the papacy funded a renewed study of antiquity. Classical proportions, domes and ordered palace façades help identify the period. These cities formed several states, not one Renaissance empire.
sourceName: National Gallery of Art · Italian Renaissance
geographyNote: Italian centres including Florence, Rome and Venice; Renaissance ideas later spread across Europe.

label: Habsburg Central Europe
summary: A dynastic union of lands developed into the Austrian Empire and, from 1867, Austria-Hungary. Palaces and planned civic avenues express changing court and state power. The family held other territories and titles before this selected Central European period.
sourceName: Schönbrunn Group · The World of the Habsburgs
geographyNote: Representative territories held at different times, not continuous Habsburg control across each modern country.

label: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
summary: The Union of Lublin joined Poland and Lithuania in a common political framework. Royal residences, churches and townscapes preserve diverse cultural patronage. The third partition in 1795 ended the Commonwealth.
sourceName: Sejm of the Republic of Poland · The Commonwealth of Two Nations
geographyNote: Representative modern locations within changing Commonwealth territories; not a map of today's national identities.

label: Industrial-age Europe
summary: Industrialisation transformed production, cities and travel at different speeds across Europe. Factories, railway stations and iron structures reveal this change alongside historic revival styles. The timeline window ends at the First World War; industrialisation continued.
sourceName: Council of Europe · European Route of Industrial Heritage
geographyNote: Representative industrial centres rather than a uniform Europe-wide starting date.
dateNote: 1750 is rounded from the mid-eighteenth century; 1914 is an editorial overview boundary, not the end of industry.

label: Modern & contemporary Europe
summary: World wars, dictatorship, reconstruction, the Cold War and European integration reshaped cities and memory. Modernist buildings, memorials and contemporary projects help read this history. This is a broad period encompassing many societies and political systems.
sourceName: House of European History · Permanent Exhibition
geographyNote: Present-day geographic reference countries; the period is not equivalent to European Union membership.
dateNote: 1914 is the selected historical turning point; the open endpoint is displayed as present.
